full_judgment:
2. The appellant along with two others was put on trial in the First Court of the Additional Sessions Judge, Khulna in Sessions Case No. 283 of 1981 for the alleged murder of one Sakhawat Hossain @ Saku of village Damodar PS Fultala, District Khulna. The appellant was charged under sections 302 and the other two were charged under Sections 302/109 Penal Code. 

 3. The deceased in injured condition allegedly made a statement to a Police Officer in the Sadar Hospital, Khulna shortly after the occurrence alleging that he was fired upon by a revolver by the appellant, his companion, while on his way back home from Khalishpur. This statement Ext. 1 was recorded as an FIR but at the trial it became relevant as a dying declaration under section 32(1) of the Evidence Act. This statement contains the entire prosecution case, sustains the order of conviction and, naturally, has been the object of trenchant criticism by the defence. There is no other evidence in this case except that of the deceased himself as far as the involvement of the appellant is concerned. The prosecution has succeeded so far in persuading the court to act upon the said statement of the deceased notwithstanding the infirmities attached to it as pointed out ceaselessly by the defence. 

 5. Prosecution case as disclosed in the statement of the deceased is, that on 25.3.81 at about 2 p.m. the deceased Sakhawat Hossain @ Saku set out from his house in village Damodar PS Fultala on his motor-cycle and went to the sawmill of the appellant at Phulbari gate within Daulatpur PS There the deceased had chats for quite some time and then his partner Humayun took him to his house at Khalishpur at about 7 p.m. There also he had talks for quite some time after which he was sent to another room of Humayun. The deceased suspected that a revolver was taken from Sabu. At about 8 p.m. the de- ceased started from the Khalishpur residence of Humayun. At that time Humayun asked the appellant to accompany the deceased up to his house. Both the deceased and the appellant left with two motor-cycles towards the house of the deceased. When they reached Sadhur Battala (Fultala PS) at about 8-30 p.m. the appellant asked the deceased to stop and as soon as the deceased stood up stopping his motorcycle, the appellant fired upon him with the revolver which hit him on the head. The deceased then left the motor cycle and started running but he fell down at a certain distance whereupon the appellant again fired two rounds hitting the deceased on the left chest and causing bleeding injuries. Seeing a van-driver nearby the deceased cried out for help and the van-driver then carried him to his house by his van. 

 7. The deceased was then taken to the Sadar Hospital Khulna at about 9-30 PM reaching there at about 10-15 p.m. and admitted in the surgical ward. A police officer from Khulna PS named Abul Hashem came to the hospital and recorded the statement of the deceased (Ext. 1) at 11-30 p.m. This statement was sent to Fultala PS on the following morning i.e. on 26.3.81 and a case was started there treating the same as an FIR. 

 8. From the Sadar hospital the deceased was taken to the Combined Military Hospital at Jessore where he died in the night following 26.3.81. PW 10 Mujibar Rahman, OC Fultala PS held inquest on the dead body of the deceased Sakhawat Hossain on the morning of 27.3.81 and sent the same through constable to Khulna Sadar Hospital for post-mortem examination. The Investigation of the case was taken up by the Circle Inspector of Police, Sadar, PW 12 Ashab Hossain, PW 13, Rezaul Karim, another Circle Inspector, Sadar submitted chargesheet against the appellant and two others under sections 302/34, Penal Code. 

 9. At the trial prosecution produced 13 witnesses. PW 1 Shahabuddin Ahmed, brother of the de-ceased, narrated the occurrence as reported to him and others by his brother at the house before he was taken to the Hospital. PW 2 Salahuddin Ahmed, the other brother of the deceased who also allegedly heard of the occurrence from the deceased, was merely tendered. PW 3 Nazrul Islam attested the dying declaration Ext. 1 and reproduced the facts in his evidence as stated therein. PW 4 a medical officer attached to Police Hospital, Khulna held the post-mortem examination of the deceased and proved three bullet injuries on his person. PW 5 is a seizure list witness and PW 6 like PW 2 was only tendered. PW 7 is the constable who carried the dead body to the morgue. PW 8 Yunus Ali and PW 9, Abdul Mazid were alleged to be the persons present at the place of occurrence at Sadhur Battala at Atrai immediately after the deceased was fired upon. They were, however, declared hostile and cross-examined by the prosecution. PWs 10 to 13 are Police Officers who were connected with the investigation of the case. 

 10. The defence case was one of denial with a further suggestion that the alleged statement of the deceased made to the police was false and fabricated and brought into existence by interested persons in collusion IA the Police Officer. 

 13. Mr. Jamiruddin Sircar, learned counsel for the appellant, submitted that the so-called dying declaration was highly doubtful and its probative value was little or nil and as such it ought not to have been relied upon for finding the appellant guilty of the grave offence of murder. He further submitted upon making reference to the various circumstances and infirmities of the prosecution case that the appellant was at least entitled to the benefit of reasonable doubt. He also argued that the High Court Division improperly ignored, to the great prejudice of the appellant, the deficiencies and weaknesses of the prosecution case in disregard of the settled norms as are applicable in a criminal case requiring the prosecution to prove by satisfactory cogent and reliable evidence the case against the accused beyond all reasonable doubt. 

 14. The learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for the State has supported the impugned judgment submitting that the High Court Division did not commit any error by ignoring the alleged infirmities relating to the dying declaration and other circumstances of the prosecution case because elaborate reasons have been given to support the findings made by it. 

 16. In the instant case the foremost criticism that has been made with regard to the alleged dying declaration is that the officer of Khulna PS, Abul Hashem who was said to have recorded the statement (Ext.1), was neither examined by the prosecution nor any explanation was given for his non-examination. It was not at all difficult to give the explanation if really there was any. The High Court Division does not seem to have given any importance to this omission of the prosecution which we do not think was right and proper. It was incumbent upon the prosecution, specially in the facts of the present case, to offer some explanation as to why Abul Hashem was not examined. If he came to depose the defence would have got an opportunity to cross-examine him and his absence has evidently deprived the defence to elicit facts which might have gone in its favour. It is not enough in a criminal case, as the High Court Division thought, that the hand-writing in Ext. 1 was proved by another police officer PW 10. In the absence of Abdul Hashem much of the scrutiny to which the statement Ext. 1 could have been subjected to was not or could not be done. None of the witnesses for the prosecution stated in their evidence as to who called Abul Hashem to the hospital and in what manner and circumstances the statement was allegedly recorded. Abdul Hashem himself, if he came to court, could say as to these things and subject himself to cross examination. Non-examination of Abut Hashem without any explanation whatever was a serious omission on the part of the prosecution which must raise the first streak of doubt as to the alleged dying declaration. 

 18. The statement Ext. 1 is found to be attested by one Abul Kashem said to be a Commissioner of the Municipality and PW 3 Nazrul Islam. Abul Kashem, a man having a better credential, was not examined and again there is no explanation for his non-examination as well. It is only PW 3 who came to prove the alleged recording of the statement made by the deceased in the hospital. He is neither related to the deceased nor had anything to do in the hospital at that hour of night. Nobody called him and on his own evidence he went inside the hospital of his own. It is highly unlikely that at that hour of night Nazrul Islam could get inside the hospital by the side of a seriously injuried patient and remain there present during all the time of recording unless he was called by somebody. From his evidence, however, it appears that he is not the person to wait for any such call and he is available for any service that an investigating agency might need at times for making up its proforma. The mere fact that his house was on the hospital road and he had a shop in front of the hospital does not give him a natural access or right to be present inside the hospital and be a witness to the dying declaration and thereby impart credibility to his evidence when the more natural, probable and competent persons such as doctors, nurses, attendents, relations, etc. are not forthcoming as witnesses. It is, therefore, very difficult in the circumstances of the case to place any reliance whatever on the evidence of PW 3. Thus the shade deepens on the doubt that has already been raised as to the genuineness of Ext. 1. 

 19. It will be seen that the statement of the deceased Ext. 1 was in the form of a long narrative giving all details. In spite of the three bullet injuries, it seems he was fit and alert enough at the time of making the statement (which is also very doubtful). However, if it were so, why then, being a literate person, his LTI was taken in the said statement ? Here again the prosecution does not offer any explanation for this unnatural conduct on the part of the deceased. One has to reckon with this circumstance keeping in view the defence suggestion that the dying declaration was a fabrication made later on after the death of the victim. The more we see the circumstances, the more we feel that the High Court Division acted improperly in disregarding all these circumstances which have rendered the alleged dying declaration to be eclipsed by gathering doubts of all kinds. The dying declaration in the circumstances of the case noticed above could only be acted upon if all the indulgences were allowed, contrary to the established practice and procedure, to the seemingly careless prosecution and the result in such a case is very likely to be a miscarriage of justice which the court, as a rule, should always avoid. 

 20. It is to be observed that in the statement of the deceased Ext. 1 there is no reference at all to any fact or circumstance from which it can be even remotely inferred that there was any reason whatever for which the appellant was likely to make an attempt on the life of the deceased. On the other hand, it appears that the appellant and the deceased were very friendly, they spent the day together immediately before the occurrence and nothing happened during the day which might have something to do with the alleged murder. The deceased did not have any reason to suspect the appellant for which he could be his possible killer. The prosecution evidence otherwise is absolutely blank on the point. In a case of this nature based only upon the dying declaration there should have been some evidence of motive although motive may not be proved in cases of direct evidence or as an ingredient of the offence. The failure of the prosecution is otherwise so overwhelming in this case that it is too much to ask for any such evidence of motive. 

 21. The deceased in his statement does not say that he met or saw any other person except the van-driver who, however, could not be traced out. Prosetution examined PWs 8 and 9 to prove that they met the deceased immediately after the occurrence. PW 8 stated in his evidence that the deceased did not state anything and so he was declared hostile. This witness also claimed that he accompanied the van carrying the deceased to his house. This part is not supported by the statement of the deceased. PW 9's evidence is still worse because he said that he did not see any injury on the deceased. In any case, their testimony does not help the prosecution at all. There is considerable mystery surrounding the facts at and after the alleged occurrence and no other reliable evidence is there to show as to how and where and by whom the deceased was actually injured. 

 22. If the so-called dying declaration Ext.1 cannot be safely relied upon then there remains for consideration the same dying declaration which was allegedly made by the deceased at his house before being taken to the hospital. There is no written record of the said statement of the deceased except as it was reproduced by PW 1 in his evidence. The prosecution is again found to be at serious fault as to this part of the case in that it did not examine any other person who were admittedly present in the house when the deceased allegedly made the statement. The mother, the sister, not even the wife of the deceased, was examined by the prosecution, let alone others, such as Haider Gazi, Tofazzal Hossain Bhuyian, Abdul Gani who are all charge-sheeted witnesses. No explanation again is given by the prose-cution for non-examination of these material witnesses. PW 13 admitted in cross-examination that Dr. Nazrul Islam Joarder, RMO, Sadar Hospital, Khulna was also a chargesheeted witness. This witness also was neither examined nor any explanation was given for his non-examination. The alleged statement of the deceased Ext. 1 becomes all the more doubtful in the absence of this Dr. Nazrul. However, the statement of the deceased said to have been made in his house is bound to give rise to the same suspicious on account of the failure of the prosecution as stated above. A question may be asked as to why the evidence of PW 1, Shahabuddin Ahmed alone should not be considered sufficient for believing the statement of the deceased made in the house. Apart from other reasons his own statement in cross-examination that he did not make any statement to the Police is sufficient to raise doubt about his veracity. He is a graduate. But he made contradictory statements in his cross-examination. While he said that he did not make any statement to the Police, he also said that he did not say to the Daroga that his brother made a statement to the police, that on 25.3.81 he told the CI at Fultala about the occurrence and then again he stated that he did not say to the police what was reported to him by his brother. It is also found that he made significant departure from what has been stated by the deceased in his alleged statement Ext. 1. To give only one example, the deceased did not say that when he fell down on the ground the appellant ran up to him, pressed him down and then fired upon him but PW 1 in his chief made such a statement. It is not necessary to refer to the other points of departure because the alleged statement of the deceased made in the house cannot be said to have been satisfactorily proved by the prosecution by all the available and reliable evidence that was at their disposal. 

 23. This is a case where the prosecution must bear the responsibility for all its laches and lapses, be they by default or by design. The case must fall for all the failures of the prosecution as noticed above. Having considered all aspects of the case, we have found it impossible to hold that the alleged dying declaration, the only piece of evidence against the appellant in this case, was free from reasonable doubt. That being so, he is entitled to the benefit of that doubt. 

 24. In the result, therefore, the appeal is al- lowed, the impugned order of conviction and sentence is set aside and the appellant is acquitted of the charge. Let the appellant Sk.Shamsur Rahman @ Shamsu be set at liberty forthwith, if not wanted in connection with any other case. 

 Latifur Rahman, J: Unfortunately, I cannot agree with the order of acquittal proposed to be delivered by my learned brother ATM Afzal, J. in this case as the orders of conviction passed by the courts below are based on oral and written dying declarations of the deceased which are also substantially corroborated by the medical evidence on record. 

 27. Appellant Shamsur Rahman alias Shamsu was convicted under section 302 of the Penal Code and sentenced to death by the Additional Sessions Judge, Khulna in Sessions Case No. 283 of 1981. The appeal of the condemned prisoner was partly allowed affirming the conviction and his sentence of death was commuted to imprisonment for life by the High Court Division, Dhaka in Criminal Appeal No. 456 of 1986. The Reference under section 374 of the Code of Criminal Procedure for confirmation of the death sentence was, however, rejected. 

 28. In this case, victim Shakhawat Hossain made a dying statement in Khulna Sadar Hospital which was subsequently treated as a First Information Report and on that basis the present case was started. The prosecution case, in brief, is that on 25.3.81 at about 2 PM victim Shakhawat Hossain went from his house at village Damoder by a motorcycle to the saw mill of appellant Shamsur Rahman at Phulbari gate of Daulatpur Police Station. There the deceased spent quite a long time in the company of accused appellant and acquitted co-accused Humayun. Thereafter Humayun invited the deceased to his house at Khalishpur. At Khalishpur the deceased reached at Humayun's house at 7 PM and remained there for some time. At one stage of the conversation they sent the victim to another room of the house of co-accused Humayun and the victim suspected that in the meanwhile co-accused Humayun borrowed a revolver from acquitted co-accused Shabu. At about 8 PM the victim started for his home when accused Humayun asked the appellant to accompany the victim by way of escorting him to his house. Then the victim along with appellant Shamsu boarded two motor-cycles and when they reached at Sadhur Battala at about 8-30 PM appellant Shamsu asked him to stop. Accordingly the victim stopped the motor cycle and as he stood up at that moment Shamsu fired a revolver shot towards him which struck on his head and the victim left the motor cycle and tried to run away when the appellant fired two successive shorts injuring him. The appellant fled away and the victim was in his senses. Hearing his cry a rickshaw van driver came and took him on his van and carried the victim to his house. In the house the victim disclosed about the occurrence before his full brothers PW 1 Shahabuddin Ahmed and PW 2 Salauddin Ahmed, sister, wife and other persons present in his house. The victim suspected that the three accused persons in conspiracy with each other shot him. At about 9-30 P.M. the victim was taken to Khulna Sadar Hospital where he reached at about 10-15 PM and at about 11-30 PM Sub-Inspector Abul Hashem of Khulna Police Station recorded his statement which he made in full senses while lying in the hospital Bed No. 11 of the surgical ward in presence of the attesting witnesses and others. After recording the statement it was read over to him and he put his LTI on his statement. Sub-Inspector Abul Hashem being a Police Officer of Khulna Police Station forwarded the said statement to the Officer-in-Charge of Fultala Police Station for treating the dying declaration as a First Information Report and to start a case on that basis as the occurrence took place within the jurisdiction of Fultala Police Station. The victim was transferred to Jessore Combined Military Hospital for better treatment and he died in the night in between 26.3.81 and 27.3.8l. The dead body of deceased Shakhawat Hossain was forwarded to morgue at Sadar Hospital, Khulna and subsequently Dr. Wahidul Islam, Doctor of Police Hospital held post mortem examination on the dead body of deceased. Investigation was held by Court Inspector PW 12 Ashab Hossain and charge sheet was submitted by his successor Court Inspector PW 13 Rezaul Karim. 

 29. The defence case was a total denial of the occurrence as alleged by the prosecution. Defence further asserted that no dying statement was made by the victim and the dying statement is a fabricated and false one. 

 30. In this case leave was granted to consider whether the High Court Division fell into an error in relying on the dying declaration Exhibit 1 by ignoring the serious and gross infirmities in upholding the conviction and sentence of the appellant in a great offence of murder under section 302 of the Pen. 

 31. Mr. Jamiruddin Sircar, learned advocate appearing for the appellant, primarily submits that the dying declaration as made in the case is inadmissible in evidence and, at any rate, the same has got little probative value as it suffers from serious infirmities and the appellant is entitled to an acquittal. Mr. Sircar has also incidentally raised some other points in his argument to which I will refer in appropriate place. 

 33. At the outset it is to be stated that the occurrence took place within Fultala Police Station and soon after the occurrence the deceased was brought home and from there he was taken to the Sadar Hospital at Khulna town where Sub-Inspector Abul Hashem, recorded the dying statement. In the present case the fact remains that Sub-Inspector Abul Hashem,who recorded the dying statement and Abul Kasem, an attesting witness, have not been examined. But one of the attesting witnesses of the dying statement, namely, PW 3 Nazrul Islam was examined in this case who heard the statement of the deceased and on oath he correctly reproduced the statement of the deceased which he heard at the time of recording of the dying statement. In this case, the Sub-Inspector of Police of Khulna Police Station is in fact not the Investigation Officer nor he has anything to do with the case as the occurrence took place under a different Police Station and he only recorded the statement of the deceased and forwarded the same to the appropriate Police Station for treating the same as a First Information Report for starting a case. In the present case the statement though made to a police officer is not made during the course of investigation and as such it is in fact immaterial as to the fact that a Police Officer recorded the dying declaration. In other words, I cannot say that he is in any way interested in the investigation or in the case itself. As a matter of fact anyone can record a dying declaration and really it is immaterial as to who recorded a dying declaration. For non-examination of such a person no exception can be taken if the same has been legally proved in accordance with law. This being the position in law, I fail to understand how it could be argued that it is obligatory to produce the person who recorded the dying declaration. For agrument's al Code. sake if in a given case, if a person who recorded the dying declaration is dead or could not be produced for any reason, then can it be argued that the same is inadmissible in evidence because the person who recorded it is not produced as a witness. It is to be kept in mind that every case is to be decided on the facts and circumstances of that given case as no two cases are alike. The objection raised relates to the non-examination of the writer of the dying statement and non-examination of an attesting witness. But I find that one of the attesting witnesses PW 3 Nazrul Islam who was present at the time of recording the dying statement proved the statement exhibit 1 of the deceased, his own signature exhibit 1/1, and the signature of Abul Kashem exhibit 1/2 on the dying statement. It was also recorded in the dying statement that the deceased on reaching home stated about the incident to his full brother PW 1 Sahabuddin Ahmed and others and this PW 1 Sahabuddin Ahmed was also present in the hospital at the time of recording of the dying statement and he also deposed that Sub-Inspector came to the hospital and recorded the statement of his victim brother in presence of PW 3 Nazrul Islam, Abul Kashem and others. PW 10 Mujibar Rahman, Officer-in-Charge of Fultala Police Station deposed that the plain paper FIR (dying declaration) was written by Sub-Inspector of Khulna Police Station Abul Hashem whose writing he knew. Mr. Sircar's argument is that since the writer, one attesting witness, the doctor and nurses were not examined, the dying declaration was not formally proved and it cannot be accepted. This objection as to the admissibility of the dying statement cannot be legally accepted as it cannot be disputed that a statement made by a person as to the cause of his death is admissible in evidence under clause(1) of section 32 of the Evidence Act. A dying declaration if reduced to writing may be proved by the person to whom it has been made or by the evidence of some person who himself himself heard it from the deceased. Thus the rule admitting a dying declaration is also subject to the rule against hearsay. Section 32 of the Evidence Act is an exception to the well known maxim- "hearsay is not evidence". It is really immaterial in the facts of the present case as to whom that declaration was made. The declaration though made to a police officer of a different police station is to be presumed to be made to a private person and for non-examination of the person who recorded this dying declaration exhibit 1, no exception is legally sustainable as to the mode of proving the dying statement. Law does not require that only the person who records the dying statement can prove it. What the law requires is that anyone who was present at the time of recording the statement can prove the dying statement. I have already held that PW 3 Nazrul Islam was not only present but was also the attesting witness of the dying statement, Ext. 1 which he has proved, besides being corroborated as to the writing by PW 10 who is acquainted with the hand writing of Abul Hashem as also by PW 1 who is said to have witnessed being present at the time of recording of the dying statement. Further, can it be argued that without examining the writer of the document and without furnishing any explanation by the prosecution for non-examining the writer of the dying statement, the same has not been formally proved in law ? It is true that prosecution has not given any explanation for not examining the person who recorded the dying statement. But law does not require that such a dying declaration cannot be considered and taken into evidence if the writer of the same be not examined for any reason. Thus in the facts of the present case, I do not find that for not giving any explanation or for not examining some witnesses, the document cannot be held to be inadmissible at all. 

 34. Next Mr. Sircar contends that why the Sub-Inspector of Police, Khulna Police Station came in the Khulna Sadar Hospital without any requisition. Normally when the condition of a victim is very serious and precarious requisition is made for recording the dying declaration by a Magistrate or by a doctor but in this case the dying statement was recorded by a police officer of a different Police Station within the course of three hours after the occurrence. It is on record that deceased Shakhawat Hossain was a student leader and he having been injured by bullet shot was brought in Khulna Sadar Hospital and hearing this if the Police Sub-Inspector of Khulna comes to hospital and records the statement can any legitimate grievance he made on that score. On hearing about such an injured person if he comes to the hospital and records the statement, I think he performs his duty as a good Police Officer as a part of his normal duty and without any contrary suggestion to P.W.1 Sahabuddin, the full brother of the victim that the said Sub-Inspector fabricated the dying declaration with the relations of the victim it would be unfair to suspect any evil motive in this regard. The dying statement was recorded at 11.30 in the night and probably the police officer though it fit to record it himself in that late night without giving any requisition to any magistrate and it is also on record that soon after recording the dying statement, the injured was sent to Jessore Combined Medical Hospital for better treatment. Thus in the facts of the case Mr. Sircar's this argument is without any substance. 

 35. Mr. Sircar next argues that the deceased was an educated person and why instead of signing his name he put his LTI on the dying declaration. In the present case the dying declaration was recorded soon after the occurrence in the hospital, that too within three hours of the occurrence and the victim gave a vivid description of the entire incident which led to the cause of his death. PW Shahabuddin, full brother of the deceased, also deposed that his brother put his LTI as he was not capable of writing at that time. Is it not stretching the argument too far to expect an injured man with bullet injuries at his arm pit to expect to sign his name instead of putting his LTI on the dying statement ? This argument is too feeble in the facts of the case. 

 36. Next, the learned Advocate argues that the injured could not have made the statement as he was physically incapacitated. It is also in evidence that the victim was taken to Jessore Combined Medical Hospital for treatment in the night of occurrence where he died 24 hours after i.e. in the night in be-tween 26.3.81 and 27.3.81. Thus he survived more than 24 hours after the assault and it is not unlikely that within three hours of the assault he could make the dying statement as testified by PW 1 Shahabuddin Ahmed and PW 3 Nazrul Islam. There is also no suggestion to these witnesses who were present at the time of recording the dying statement including the medicial officer who held post mortem examination that the deceased was physically incapable of making such a statement. Further the statement that has been recorded in the present case is in the words of the victim and this also shows that Saku had the physical capacity to make the statement. The prosecution having not suggested to PW 1 and PW 3 who were present at the time of recording of the statement that the deceased was incapable of making the dying statement, and there being no cross-examination to Doctor PW 4 Dr. Wahidul Islam who held post mortern examination that the deceased could not have talked after he received such bullet injuries, it is really difficult for me to guess and surmise that the deceased was incapable of making this statement. It is also difficult for me to accept this argument or Mr. Sircar when there is no evidence on record in this regard. The statement Exhibit 1 was recorded within three hours of the occurrence and the statement having been read over to the victim, he admitted the correctness of the same while in full senses and put his LTI on the same. In this connection, I may point out that there are many cases in which more extensive and severe injuries were sustained by the victims, yet they had the power of volitional act and in many cases the victims were able to perform some act as that of walking or speaking and survived for some hours or days after receiving very grave injuries, which would ordinarily have proved fatal. It is on record that the victim survived more than 24 hours after the occurrence and as such internal injuries were injuries which would not have impaired the power of speech and senses of the victim completely. The dying declaration as made by the victim is also in his own narrative and not at any response to any leading question and the same also goes to show that this was not made by any prompting from outside or being tutored by and person. This statement was recorded exactly in the words of victim Shakhawat Hossain without being assisted by any interested person. There is no suggestion to the witnesses who were present at the time of recording the dying declaration that the statement was a tutored and prompted one and the same was supplied to the victim by anybody. Since this is the version of the victim it is indeed a valuable evidence and I have already indicated that the victim was capable of making the statement as such. 

 37. Mr. Sircar next argued that in the present case prosecution has failed to ascribe any motive. At the outset I want to say that in a criminal case motive is not very relevant though the prosecution can prove motive in a case. In the dying statement it was said that Humayun was the partner of the victim and he took the victim to his house. The victim suspected that the three appellants in conspiracy shot him. I do not find anything else as to the motive of the assault in the statement. Further, in the dying statement if the victim would have said anything regarding motive of this assault that would not have been very relevant as it is not a statement as to the cause of his death. Can a case of such a nature based on oral and written dying declarations be disbelieved merely because no motive is proved by the prosecution. 

 38. Mr. Sircar also argues that PW 3 Nazrul Islam is a chance witness and he should not be believed to be present at the time of recording of the dying statement. It appears from the deposition of PW 3 that his house is at the hospital road and he has also a shop in the hospital road. He was present in the hospital at 11-30 in the night of occurrence where hearing that a patient was brought with bullet injuries he went there to see him. Soon thereafter the Sub-Inspector of Khulna came and recorded the statement. The evidence of P.W.3 shows that he was a natural witness having a shop and residence in front of the hospital and hearing that a victim with bullet injury was brought in hospital it was not unnatural for him to be present in the hospital at the time of recording the dying declaration. His evidence cannot be brushed aside or viewed with suspicion on the ground that he is a chance witness. It is a common knowledge in our country that on getting such news people very often assemble as we are more informal and casual. In the context that PW 3 does not know either the deceased nor the appellant how it could he argued that he was deposing falsely in the case. The learned Advocate argues that the dying declaration was recorded in the presence of his full brother PW 1 Shahabuddin Ahmed and as such it should not be believed. If the presence of a full brother in such a condition be considered to be a ground for suspicion on account of relationship, as argued by Mr. Sircar, I think most of the dying statements would have to be discarded. 

 39. The learned Advocate further points out the dying declaration does not show that PW 1 was a witness to the same. It is true that in the dying declaration PW 1 was not mentioned as witness but the names of two other attesting witnesses have been mentioned including PW 3 Nazrul Islam. Thus, the non-mentioning of the name of PW 1 as a witness is not very material in the facts of the present case when PW1 himself deposed that he brought his brother to the hospital and he was present althrough during the time of recording of the dying declaration. 

 40. There is a very important and vital aspect in the case that co-accused Humayun, as stated in the dying declaration, was the partner of the victim and the victim spent a long time in the company of appellant and other co-accused before the occurrence. Both the victim and the appellant were coining in the night of occurrence by two motor-cycles. Both the appellant and the victim were known from before and they were alone coming by two motor-cycles in the night of occurrence. The prosecution case is that the appellant told the deceased to stop his motor-cycle and soon thereafter he fired from his revolver. Thus about the identity of the appellant there is no difficulty and in the statement there is nothing to show that the deceased on his own had any enmity or hostility with the appellant and as such it cannot be argued that the deceased will falsely implicate the appellant in this case. The defence has also not suggested in cross-examination to any witnesses regarding any apparent enmity with the deceased. Further, no other person was present in the company of the deceased when the assault was made other than the appellant. About the identity there could not be any question as they were known from before and were coming together in the night of occurrence. The defence only denied the occurrence without suggesting as to how the deceased died. 

 41. Mr. Sircar also points out that the rickshaw van driver who carried the victim to his house soon after the occurrence has not been examined. The rickshaw van driver is not a material witness in the facts of the present case. The omission to examine the rickshaw van driver is too insignificant in the face of the dying declaration. 

 42. Next, he contends that why there is no doctor's certificate in the dying declaration, Ext. 1. In the facts of the present case Doctor's certificate was not necessary as the victim himself gave a long narrative of the incident and thereafter put his LTI on the same after admitting the correctness of the same. The dying statement shows that it was read over to the victim who was in his full senses at that moment of giving the statement. 

 43. Mr. Sircar having failed to shake the case on broad aspect, argued that why a doctor of police hospital will hold the post mortem examination of the deceased. From the post mortem report it appears that the post mortem was held in the morgue by a doctor of police hospital which was certified by the Civil Surgeon of Khulna. I think no lawful exception can be taken for this post mortem examination. 

 44. In the present case apart from the written dying declaration of the deceased, there is the oral dying statement of the deceased to his brothers and others. 

 47. Mr. Sircar pointed out that PW 8 Yunus Ali and PW 9 Abdul Majid were declared hostile. It. appears that they were cross-examined by the defence. PW 8 testified that at the time of occurrence on 25.3.81 he was a tenant in the house of Ishaque Master at Atrai and at 8-30 PM he heard cries 'save me—save me' and he came out on the verandah and saw Saku (victim) fall down on the verandah with injuries on head and other parts of the body and he shouted out. PW 9 Abdul Majid and others came and that he recognised the vitim as Saku and he was carried in a cycle rickshaw van to his house. This witness PW 8 stated that Saku stated nothing to him and at this stage he was declared hostile by the prosecution. PW 9 Abdul Majid also stated that hearing hue and cry of PW 8 he came out from his grocery shop near the place of occurrence and recognised the victim, but he stated that he did not see any injury and at that time he was declared hostile by the prosecution. These two witnesses though not eye-witnesses of the occurrence are material witnesses about the time, place and manner of occurrence being the earliest persons who saw the victim and put the victim in cycle rickshaw van. The defence, of course, did not croscexamine these witnesses with regard to the time, place and manner of occurrence. Thus the evidence of these two hostile witnesses cannot be rejected either in whole or in part but the whole of the evidence so far it affects both favourably and unfavourably must be taken into consideration in the present case. 

 49. The learned Advocate also made a point for not examining the wife, sister and others to whom the deceased made the oral declaration. I may point out here that it is for the prosecution to decide which witnesses the prosecution wants to produce but for non-examination of any eye-witness or for that matter any material witnesses, of course, an adverse inference can be drawn against the prosecution under section 114(g) of the Evidence Act. In the present case, since the conviction is based on oral and writ-ten dying declarations, I do not think that the witnesses, as pointed out by Mr. Sircar, arc material witnesses in the facts of the present case. Of the inmates of the house a full brother PW I Shahabuddin Ahmed has been examined by the prosecution and another full brother PW 2 Salahuddin Ahmed was tendered by the prosecution and defence declined to cross-examine him. About wife and sister of the deceased it could not have been said that they could have given any further information than what had been furnished in the dying declaration of the victim himself. As a matter of fact in a case of this nature the evidence of those witnesses would not have helped in proving the prosecution case as the basis of the conviction is the dying declaration. Further, prosecution is also not bound to produce all witnesses. The witnesses whom the prosecution think that will not support its case, the prosecution can omit them. The real test is whether in the facts of this case, the witnesses, as pointed out by Mr. Sircar, are material witnesses to prove the prosecution case. There being no eye-witnesses in the case and there being only dying declaration of the victim himself, I do not think that Mr. Sircar can legitimately argue that the witnesses are material witnesses in the facts of the present case. The learned Advocate has also not argued regarding any prejudice for non-examination of the person who recorded the dying declaration of deceased Shakhwat Hossain. In the four corners of the paper book there is not a word of prejudice non-examining the writer of the dying statement Mr. Sircar has not deliberately argued this because the cross-examination which could have been made to the writer of the dying declaration, if examined, had not been at all made to PW 1, PW 3 and PW 10, who were examined to prove Exhibit 1. 

 50. Thus I am constrained to say that on broad feature no infirmity could be pointed out in the writ-ten dying declaration and the mode of proof of the same. The omissions pointed out by the learned Advocate for the appellant are really of no worth in the context of the present case and I find that dying statement, Ext. 1, is essentially true and genuine. Regarding the credibility of the dying declaration, there is nothing on record to suggest that it was a product of prompting from outside or that someone persuaded the victim to substitute the appellant for his real assailant. Rather the dying statement was made when the victim was possessed of his full senses. Since there is no chance of mistake on the part of the victim in identifying the very known appellant and there being no inconsistency with the other evidence and circumstances of the case, I believe the same to be the truthful version of the deceased. 

 51. The prosecution in the facts of the case has produced the best evidence which the prosecution could have led in the present case and on the basis of that, the case against the appellant has been proved beyond the shadow of reasonable doubt. Before parting with the case. I must say that the learned advocate for the appellant has failed to assail the positive evidence that has been adduced by the prosecution in the case and, on the contrary, his whole approach to the case is in the negative, as to why some witnesses have not been examined, as to why motive has not been proved, so on and so forth. I am afraid such argument on the part of the learned advocate cannot be entertained in the facts of the present case, when he totally failed to assail the dying statements both oral and written in the case. 

 Thus, on a careful consideration of the evidence, facts and circumstances of the case, I hold that the courts below have rightly convicted the appellant under section 302 of the Penal Code. Accordingly, the appeal is dismissed.
